items.title: Celebrating 20 Years of Open Movies
items.summary_original: This year we are celebrating 20 years of making Open Movies. 17 titles, all different and beautiful in their own way. And in the spirit of sharing and being open, visitors of the exhibition can take a frame with them. 20 years of Open Movies exhibition at Blender Conference 2026 Thank you for doing your part. Let’s see what the next decade of open filmmaking will bring!

items.title: Synthetic users are making me rethink “imperfect research”
items.summary_original: Why I’m reconsidering a principle I’ve believed for years. I’ve always believed that imperfect research is better than no research at all. Synthetic users have made me reconsider that. When synthetic responses are treated like findings from real users, they can create something far more dangerous than uncertainty: false confidence. What I mean by “imperfect research” Until synthetic users entered the picture, “imperfect research” still meant some contact with the thing you were trying to understand: actual users, their behavior, and their experiences. Maybe the sample is small, recruitment is messy, or the prototype is rough. Sometimes you only have time for five interviews. These limitations matter. items.summary_de: Warum ich ein Prinzip überdenke, an das ich seit Jahren geglaubt habe. Ich habe immer geglaubt, dass unvollständige Forschung besser ist als gar keine Forschung. Synthetische Benutzer haben mich dazu gebracht, das zu überdenken. Wenn synthetische Antworten wie Erkenntnisse echter Benutzer behandelt werden, können sie etwas weitaus Gefährlicheres als Unsicherheit erzeugen: falsches Vertrauen. Was ich mit „unvollkommener Forschung“ meine: Bis synthetische Benutzer ins Spiel kamen, bedeutete „unvollkommene Forschung“ immer noch einen gewissen Kontakt mit dem, was Sie verstehen wollten: tatsächliche Benutzer, ihr Verhalten und ihre Erfahrungen. Sie beeinflussen Ihre Schlussfolgerungen, aber eines bleibt wahr: Sie haben einen beobachtet oder mit ihm gesprochen

items.title: liam de la bedoyere’s inflatable chopsticks roll up into your pocket between meals
items.summary_original: POPSTICKS REIMAGINES CHOPSTICKS AS INFLATABLE UTENSILS Some ideas begin with a serious problem. Popsticks begins with the possibility of finding yourself without chopsticks, which is apparently enough to justify a little design intervention. Created by designer Liam de la Bedoyere, the playful concept proposes a pair of inflatable chopsticks that can be rolled up, slipped into a pocket, and brought out when dinner calls. Instead of folding through hinges or coming apart into smaller pieces, the utensils rely on air to take shape. The concept is as straightforward as it is unexpected. items.title: 50 years on, here's why TypoCircle still matters, and deserves celebrating
items.summary_original: Run by volunteers since 1976, the organisation is marking its half century with £15 posters by Paula Scher, Margaret Calvert and more. To rank-and-file creative workers, some big design organisations can feel remote, both in terms of distance and overall attitude. But TypoCircle is different. For many members, the organisation actually has a visible, marked presence in their homes. That's because for decades now, everyone who's attended a TypoCircle talk has gone home with a poster designed by that evening's speaker. And those posters have spread across the country's living rooms, studios and, according to its chairwoman Louise Sloper, its toilets. items.title: A Practical Guide To Naming Things
items.summary_original: Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables. Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic , so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific , leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.
